steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our theory paper on the memorization capacity of multi-head attention in transformers. Motivate why memorization matters, summarize what is known for fully connected networks, explain why we focus on an attention-only single-layer MHA module, and list our contributions (assumptions, capacity result, proof idea, experiments).

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation
- transformers: de-facto architecture, state-of-the-art in NLP and vision; recent breakthroughs
- billions of parameters
- question: how effectively do they memorize training data?
- matters for privacy; stepping stone to quantifying generalization
- insight into roles of different building blocks

2. Memorization capacity / FCNs
- definition: minimal set of parameters {\bm{\mathcal{W}}} such that f_{\bm{\mathcal{W}}}(\bm{x})=\bm{y} for all training pairs (\bm{x},\bm{y})
- FCNs studied extensively; back to at least the 1980s: first results for single-hidden-layer Threshold networks, binary labels
- best known bound for single-hidden-layer ReLU FCNs established only recently, after numerous studies
- extensions to deeper models
- still only order-wise bounds, unknown constants, logarithmic factors
- most assume continuous inputs in “General Position”: mild, holds under small random perturbations

3. Transformers
- memorization capacity of transformers: in its infancy
- architecture: (i) Multi-head Attention (MHA) module, (ii) ReLU fully-connected network
- MHA: convex combinations of inputs via softmax similarities; unique vs FCNs; selective attention, long sequences
- theory largely unexplored -> we study memorization capacity of MHA
- isolate from ReLU FCN -> Attention-only models

4. Setting and contributions
- single-layer MHA, H heads; inputs: n\times d key/context matrix (n tokens) and d\times 1 query vector
- question: effect of number of heads and context size on memorization
- assumptions: more relaxed than General Position; query vectors Kruskal rank at least n; context vectors of each example linearly independent; validated on ViT etc. after a single layer (Attention-only or full Transformer, random or pretrained); General-Position fails there
- result: H heads, embedding dim d, key/query dim d_{h}, value dim d_{v}, context size n<d, output dim {d_{\text{out}}}\leq d_{v}, O(Hd(d_{h}+d_{v})) params -> memorizes \Omega\left(H\min(n,d_{h})\right) examples; with {d_{\text{out}}}=d_{h}=d and n=\Theta(d) recovers optimal order
- proof: heads take distinct roles, softmax allocates; each head “responsible” for \min(n,d_{h})-1 examples; saturation of softmax + key-query weight adjustments; minimal interference
- experiments: validate assumptions; synthetic: effect of H, n, d_{h}; saturation of softmax

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Transformers are now the de-facto architecture for getting state-of-the-art performance in different domains such as natural language processing and vision tasks, as recent breakthroughs show. These models are huge, often with billions of parameters, which they need to reach their high performance. Because of their size and complexity, a natural question comes up: how well can they memorize the training data? This question is important from a privacy perspective, and also as a stepping stone toward quantifying how well the model can generalize to new data. Also, studying how memorization emerges in transformers can give insights into the different roles that their different building blocks play.

Concretely, the memorization capacity of a model f_{\bm{\mathcal{W}}} is the minimal set of parameters {\bm{\mathcal{W}}} such that f_{\bm{\mathcal{W}}}(\bm{x})=\bm{y} holds for all input-output pairs (\bm{x},\bm{y}) in the training dataset. This question has been analyzed a lot for fully connected networks (FCNs), going back to at least the 1980s, when early work proved the first results for single-hidden-layer Threshold networks with binary labels. The best known bound on the memorization capacity of single-hidden-layer ReLU FCNs was only established recently by another study, after many other recent studies. Recent studies also looked a lot at extensions to deeper models. But for now the best known results are order-wise bounds, with unknown constants and logarithmic factors. Most of these works on memorization of FCNs assume continuous inputs in “General Position,” which is a fairly mild assumption, since it holds for example under small random perturbations of the input examples.

Compared to FCNs, understanding the memorization capacity of transformers is still in its infancy. A common Transformer architecture has two main parts: (i) a Multi-head Attention (MHA) module and (ii) a ReLU fully-connected network. The MHA module makes convex combinations of its input elements by computing softmax similarities between the input representations. This operation is unique to transformers compared to FCNs, and it is used in practice because it can selectively attend to information from different representations and process long sequences effectively. But its theoretical underpinnings are still mostly unexplored. This paper tries to help close this gap by studying the memorization capacity of the MHA module. To separate its role from the ReLU FCN, we take a step toward analyzing Attention-only models.

4. Setting and contributions
- single-layer MHA, H heads; n\times d key/context matrix of n tokens, d\times 1 query vector
- question: effect of number of heads and context size
- relaxed assumptions: Kruskal rank at least n for query vectors; linearly independent context vectors; validated on ViT etc.; General-Position fails
- bound: O(Hd(d_{h}+d_{v})) params -> \Omega\left(H\min(n,d_{h})\right) examples; optimal order when {d_{\text{out}}}=d_{h}=d and n=\Theta(d)
- proof idea: each head “responsible” for \min(n,d_{h})-1 examples; softmax saturation; minimal interference
- experiments: assumptions; H, n, d_{h}; softmax saturation

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Transformers are now the de-facto architecture for getting state-of-the-art performance in different domains such as natural language processing and vision tasks, as recent breakthroughs show. These models are huge, often with billions of parameters, which they need to reach their high performance. Because of their size and complexity, a natural question comes up: how well can they memorize the training data? This question is important from a privacy perspective, and also as a stepping stone toward quantifying how well the model can generalize to new data. Also, studying how memorization emerges in transformers can give insights into the different roles that their different building blocks play.

Concretely, the memorization capacity of a model f_{\bm{\mathcal{W}}} is the minimal set of parameters {\bm{\mathcal{W}}} such that f_{\bm{\mathcal{W}}}(\bm{x})=\bm{y} holds for all input-output pairs (\bm{x},\bm{y}) in the training dataset. This question has been analyzed a lot for fully connected networks (FCNs), going back to at least the 1980s, when early work proved the first results for single-hidden-layer Threshold networks with binary labels. The best known bound on the memorization capacity of single-hidden-layer ReLU FCNs was only established recently by another study, after many other recent studies. Recent studies also looked a lot at extensions to deeper models. But for now the best known results are order-wise bounds, with unknown constants and logarithmic factors. Most of these works on memorization of FCNs assume continuous inputs in “General Position,” which is a fairly mild assumption, since it holds for example under small random perturbations of the input examples.

Compared to FCNs, understanding the memorization capacity of transformers is still in its infancy. A common Transformer architecture has two main parts: (i) a Multi-head Attention (MHA) module and (ii) a ReLU fully-connected network. The MHA module makes convex combinations of its input elements by computing softmax similarities between the input representations. This operation is unique to transformers compared to FCNs, and it is used in practice because it can selectively attend to information from different representations and process long sequences effectively. But its theoretical underpinnings are still mostly unexplored. This paper tries to help close this gap by studying the memorization capacity of the MHA module. To separate its role from the ReLU FCN, we take a step toward analyzing Attention-only models.

Concretely, we study a single-layer MHA module with H heads. Its inputs are a n\times d key/context matrix made of the representations of n tokens, and a d\times 1 query vector. We especially want to understand how the number of attention heads and the context size of the input affect memorization in this architecture. Our contributions are:

- We introduce a new set of assumptions on the input data that are more relaxed than General Position assumptions. The first assumption needs the set of all query vectors to have Kruskal rank at least n, and the second needs the context vectors of each example to be linearly independent. We motivate and validate these with experiments on real-world models like ViT, after a single layer, whether Attention-only or a complete Transformer, randomly initialized or pretrained. General-Position, on the other hand, does not hold in any of these settings.

- Under these practically relevant assumptions, we prove that a single-layer MHA module with H heads, embedding dimension d, key/query dimension d_{h}, value dimension d_{v}, context size n<d, output dimension {d_{\text{out}}}\leq d_{v}, with a total of O(Hd(d_{h}+d_{v})) trainable parameters, can memorize \Omega\left(H\min(n,d_{h})\right) input examples. In particular when {d_{\text{out}}}=d_{h}=d and n=\Theta(d), this result recovers the optimal order of real-valued numbers that can be memorized with this number of parameters.

- Our proof shows how different attention heads play different roles in memorizing different sets of examples, and how the softmax helps with this allocation of roles. To show that memory capacity grows linearly with H, the idea is to make each head individually “responsible” for memorizing \min(n,d_{h})-1 examples. Using the saturation property of softmax and specific key-query weight adjustments, we design the softmax logits we want for individual heads while making sure there is minimal interference with other examples.

- Besides the experiments validating our assumptions on the input sequences, we design and discuss synthetic experiments that support our findings: the impact of head number H, context length n and key/query dimension d_{h} on memorization, and also the occurrence of the saturation property of the softmax operator.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Transformers have emerged as the de-facto architecture for state-of-the-art performance across domains such as natural language processing and vision tasks, as demonstrated by recent breakthroughs, e.g. [1,2,3]. These models are characterized by their immense scale, often comprising billions of parameters to achieve high performance. Given their size and complexity, a natural question arises: How effectively can they memorize the training data? This question is important both from a privacy perspective [4] and as a stepping stone towards quantifying the model's ability to generalize to new data [5]. In addition, studying how memorization emerges in transformers can offer insights into the distinct roles of their different building blocks.

Concretely, the memorization capacity of a model f_{\bm{\mathcal{W}}} refers to the minimal set of parameters {\bm{\mathcal{W}}} such that f_{\bm{\mathcal{W}}}(\bm{x})=\bm{y} holds for all input-output pairs (\bm{x},\bm{y}) in the training dataset. Historically, this question has been analyzed extensively for fully connected networks (FCNs), dating back to at least the 1980s, when [10] proved the first set of results for single-hidden-layer Threshold networks with binary labels. The best known bound on the memorization capacity of single-hidden-layer ReLU FCNs was established only recently by [11], following numerous recent studies, e.g. [5,12]. Extensions to deeper models have also been considered extensively, e.g. [13,14,15,12]. However, the best known results so far are order-wise bounds, involving unknown constants and logarithmic factors. Most of these works on memorization of FCNs assume continuous inputs in “General Position,” a relatively mild assumption that holds, for instance, under small random perturbations of the input examples.

In contrast to FCNs, our understanding of the memorization capacity of transformers is still in its infancy. A common Transformer architecture consists of two main components: (i) a Multi-head Attention (MHA) module and (ii) a ReLU fully-connected network. The MHA module creates convex combinations of its input elements by computing softmax similarities between input representations. This operation, unique to transformers compared to FCNs, is leveraged in practice for its ability to selectively attend to information from various representations and to process long sequences effectively [16]. Yet its theoretical underpinnings remain largely unexplored. This paper aims to help close this gap by investigating the memorization capacity of the MHA module. To isolate its role from that of the ReLU FCN, we take a step toward analyzing Attention-only models.

Concretely, we study a single-layer MHA module with H heads that takes as inputs a n\times d key/context matrix comprising representations of n tokens and a d\times 1 query vector. We are particularly interested in how the number of attention heads and the context size of the input affect memorization in this architecture. Our contributions are as follows:

\bullet We introduce a new set of input-data assumptions that are more relaxed than General Position assumptions. Our first assumption requires the set of all query vectors to have Kruskal rank at least n, and our second requires the context vectors of each example to be linearly independent. These are motivated and validated by experiments on real-world models, such as ViT, following a single layer, whether Attention-only or a complete Transformer, either randomly initialized or pretrained. In contrast, General-Position does not hold in either of these settings.

\bullet Under this set of practically relevant assumptions, we prove that a single-layer MHA module with H heads, embedding dimension d, key/query dimension d_{h}, value dimension d_{v}, context size n<d, output dimension {d_{\text{out}}}\leq d_{v}, and a total of O(Hd(d_{h}+d_{v})) trainable parameters, can memorize \Omega\left(H\min(n,d_{h})\right) input examples. In particular, when {d_{\text{out}}}=d_{h}=d and n=\Theta(d), this result recovers the optimal order of real-valued numbers that can be memorized with the given number of parameters.

\bullet Our proof shows how different attention heads play distinct roles in memorizing different sets of examples, and how the softmax facilitates this role allocation. To show that memory capacity increases linearly with H, our idea is to make each head individually “responsible” for memorizing \min(n,d_{h})-1 examples. By leveraging the saturation property of softmax and introducing specific key-query weight adjustments, we design the desired softmax logits for individual heads while ensuring minimal interference with other examples.

\bullet In addition to experiments validating our assumptions on the input sequences, we design and discuss synthetic experiments that corroborate our findings: namely, the impact of the head number H, context length n and key/query dimension d_{h} on memorization, as well as the occurrence of the saturation property of the softmax operator.
